subject: radiology
title: Central venous catheters: choice and line care

steps.tx: Catheter tip position decides safety, because high caval flow dilutes drugs and discourages clot formation around the tip. The **catheter tip** should rest at the **cavoatrial junction**, where the cava meets the atrium under fluoroscopy. The **right internal jugular vein** offers the straightest run toward that junction with the lowest thrombosis risk. Left sided and femoral lines kink and clot sooner, so the team reserves those routes for a blocked right side. A tip that sits too deep triggers arrhythmia, while a shallow tip in a brachiocephalic vein clots fast.

steps.tx: This chest fluoroscopy image shows a catheter that enters through the **right internal jugular vein** and travels down the cava. The tip rests exactly at the **cavoatrial junction**, where fast flow dilutes infused drugs and discourages clot around the tip. The label for **high flow dilution** explains why a shallow or deep tip causes trouble after placement. The image matters for the exam because tip confirmation precedes vesicant infusion in every central line case. A deep tip risks arrhythmia while a shallow tip clots and fails early.

steps.tx: Device choice follows treatment duration, because infection and thrombosis risks grow differently across catheter types. An **implanted port** suits intermittent chemotherapy over months, with needle access through skin and low infection rates. A **tunnelled cuffed catheter** serves dialysis and daily infusions, where the cuff forms a barrier against skin organisms. A **PICC line** covers weeks of antibiotics through arm veins, although clot rates run higher than jugular routes. Duration therefore picks the device, with ports for months, tunnels for daily needs and arm lines for weeks.

An implanted port suits intermittent chemotherapy over months with needle access through skin safely. A tunnelled cuffed catheter serves dialysis and daily infusions where the cuff bars skin organisms. An arm line covers weeks of antibiotics through arm veins although clot rates run higher. Duration therefore picks the device with ports for months and tunnels for daily needs.

steps.tx: Line infection usually starts at the hub, so daily handling matters as much as insertion technique itself. **Aseptic hub care** with scrubbed connections and antiseptic dressings prevents most infections during routine ward use. Fever with line tenderness earns **paired blood cultures** from line and periphery before antibiotics start in hospital. An uncomplicated infection may clear with locks and systemic drugs while a tunnelled line stays in place. **Tunnel abscess or fungaemia** demands removal because organisms coat plastic permanently and relapse follows retention inevitably.

steps.tx: A blocked line speaks through pressures and flow pattern, and each pattern points toward a different remedy. A **fibrin sheath** wraps the tip and allows infusion but blocks withdrawal, so low dose lytic dwells clear it. **Catheter related thrombosis** swells the arm or neck, and duplex mapped clot needs anticoagulation with line review. **Pinch off syndrome** cracks a subclavian line at the costoclavicular angle and warns through positional flow changes. Every blockage forces a remove versus salvage judgement that weighs infection, clot and ongoing need together.
